author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Tensions remain high in Portadown, Northern Ireland, as residents of Garvaghy Road prepare for further protests over a planned Orange Order parade through their predominantly Catholic, nationalist community.

Hundreds of residents blocked the road after a High Court gave the Protestant Orange Order permission to parade through the area, something that has not happened there for almost 30 years. Drumcree was the scene of intense sectarian violence and protests in the 1990s, before the Good Friday Agreement.

Negotiations are under way involving the Garvaghy Road community, Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant and representatives of the Protestant community and Orange Order. Catholic residents say allowing the parade could undermine the peace that has endured for decades, while the Orange Order argues its legal right to parade should not be blocked by what it describes as an unlawful protest.

Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith reports from Portadown, Northern Ireland.

title: Northern Ireland Orange Order march: Tensions remain over planned Garvaghy Road parade

Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate says Africa is paying a high price for a crisis it did not create. She has taken her fight for climate justice from the streets of Kampala to the halls of power. She has been front and centre in the global climate movement, urging world leaders to act, taking part in protests and speaking at international conferences about the dangers of global warming.

However, Nakate admits progress has been slow. As a UNICEF goodwill ambassador, she has seen firsthand how communities are affected, and insists the major polluters should be held accountable. She is determined to raise awareness about how global warming is affecting African countries in particular. She says the continent is often left out of discussions.

Nakate admits she sometimes feels hopeless about the state of the world, but she is encouraged by grassroots initiatives that are bringing about change.

description:
In 1955, 29 newly independent nations met in Bandung, Indonesia and terrified the world’s superpowers. This is the story of what happened next.
Having rejected colonial rule, they set out to break free from a system built against them. The meeting became a movement, one that shaped leaders from Nelson Mandela to Malcolm X and reshaped the Global South’s sense of its own power.
But the empires struck back with coups, economic pressure and years of breaking the unity that was built. The idea, however, never died.
Told through rare archival footage and expert analysis, this film asks why Bandung’s questions about power and sovereignty are just as urgent now as they were then.

More than 2,000 people are sheltering at a displacement centre in Bangkok’s eastern suburb of Lat Krabang after severe flooding left surrounding areas under water. The centre has expanded rapidly, with only a few hundred people there 24 hours earlier, while more residents continue to arrive. Although heavy rains have stopped, floodwaters have not receded and remain as high as one metre in some areas. The displaced are being provided with food, bedding, mosquito nets and medical supplies, but officials warn they may have to remain at the centre for up to seven days. High water levels in the ground are preventing floodwater from draining, delaying the return home and the clean-up effort. 

Al Jazeera’s Tony Cheng reports from Lat Krabang, Bangkok.

description:
More than 100 young people are taking part in a Youth Technology Hackathon in Gaza City, presenting more than 45 projects designed to address challenges in their communities. Among them is a robot developed by 14-year-old Bassam Harara that can enter damaged buildings and inspect them remotely, potentially reducing risks to people. Another team has developed a gesture-controlled robot to assist elderly people and those with disabilities with everyday tasks. Other projects focus on smart farming, water treatment and technology-based solutions to shortages affecting daily life. But the young inventors face major obstacles in turning their ideas into working projects, including unreliable electricity and the high cost and limited availability of mechatronics equipment. Despite those constraints, the hackathon is giving a new generation of Gazans a space to experiment, build and imagine a different future. 

Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili reports from Gaza City, Palestine.

description: Supporters of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan have postponed planned protests in Islamabad after authorities banned public gatherings and blocked major roads, but heavy security measures remain in place across the capital and surrounding areas. Thousands of containers have been deployed to block roads leading into Islamabad, disrupting transport and leaving truck drivers facing major financial losses. Sources told Al Jazeera that about 1,500 containers are in Islamabad and another 2,000 have been deployed in nearby cities, towns and roads in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. With each container costing about $70 a day to rent, the government is spending close to $250,000 daily on the barriers alone. An estimated 16,000 to 18,000 security personnel have also been deployed, taking the reported daily cost of the security operation to more than $300,000 when food and other expenses are included. author: Al Jazeera English
description:
At least 14 people have died when heavy rain and storms triggered flooding and landslides in Nepal.
Local authorities say at least 11 people are missing and warned of more possible flash floods.

It's been a month since catastrophic floods tore through Nepal. At least 14,000 people were killed, and 5,285 people are still missing. And while families work to recover from their losses, thousands of children are still without reliable access to clean water. 
Fresh rains are now worsening conditions for the more than 1,100 displaced families living in temporary shelters.
And it's estimated to cost the country more than $4bn to start to rebuild.

Prasen Khati is the director of influencing, campaigns and communications at Plan International Nepal. He says the floods come at a difficult time as the country continues to deal with the devastation of August's flash floods.
